_runtime_sources: A balance sheet shows what the business owns, what it owes and the owner’s recorded interest at a particular date. Its main groups are assets, liabilities and equity. It explains financial position, while a profit and loss statement explains performance over a period.
A better rhythm for your books.

A bookkeeper can coordinate with your tax preparer when that work is included in the agreed service. The bookkeeper organizes and explains the records, while the tax preparer determines tax treatment and filing requirements. Clear responsibilities make the handoff easier and reduce repeated requests for the same information.

A bookkeeper can organize expenses, explain their recorded categories and flag potential deductions for tax review. Whether a particular expense qualifies for a deduction depends on tax rules, the business purpose and supporting facts. Your tax professional determines the appropriate tax treatment using those records.

A bookkeeper maintains the transaction records that help a business understand its finances. The work can include organizing income and expenses, reconciling accounts, reviewing unpaid invoices and bills, and preparing reports from the completed records. The exact responsibilities should be defined in the service agreement.

A cleared transaction has appeared in the bank or card provider’s posted activity. That does not necessarily mean the transaction has completed a formal reconciliation in your bookkeeping software. Clearing identifies movement at the financial institution, while reconciliation checks a complete statement period against the books.

A large uncategorized balance usually means the books lack enough information or consistent rules to identify transactions properly. Unfamiliar merchant descriptions, incomplete receipts, new payment systems and mixed business and personal spending can all contribute. The solution starts with finding the recurring cause, not assigning everything to miscellaneous expense.

A monthly bookkeeping close is a practical way for a business to keep balances checked and reports current. The amount of work depends on transaction volume and complexity, so a quiet business may need a simpler routine than a growing one. Records still need to support income, expenses and account balances throughout the year.

A monthly bookkeeping review can reveal duplicate payments, unfamiliar vendors, missing receipts and unusual account movements. It cannot guarantee that fraud will be detected. A routine review is most useful when transactions are supported and the owner also oversees access and payment approvals.

A negative card balance in bookkeeping software can represent a real credit, a display convention or a recording error. Start by checking how the software presents credit card liabilities and compare the balance with the card statement for the same date. Do not assume a minus sign always means the business owes money.
A notebook for running your business.

A payment from your business bank account to a business credit card normally reduces the card liability and the bank balance. It is not another expense if the individual card purchases are already recorded. Record purchases, payments, interest and fees according to what each transaction actually represents.

A payment posted to the wrong account should be traced to its source and corrected without creating a second payment. First clarify whether the error concerns the bank account, expense category, customer record or vendor record. Each changes a different part of the books.

A profit and loss statement shows revenue and expenses for a period, a balance sheet shows assets and obligations at a date, and a cash flow statement explains changes in cash. Together, monthly financial reports show profitability, financial position and cash movement. They provide more context than the bank balance alone.

A profitable business can have low cash because profit and cash measure different things. Customers may not have paid yet, inventory or equipment may have absorbed money, and loan repayments or owner withdrawals may reduce cash without appearing as ordinary expenses. The accounting basis also affects when profit is reported.
A refund needs to be recorded

A supplier refund commonly reduces the related expense or asset cost, or clears a supplier credit, depending on the original purchase and reason for the refund. Link it to the original record and supporting credit note. Do not automatically categorize it as sales income because money entered the bank.

A transaction entered in the wrong year can shift income, expenses or balances between reporting periods. Review the underlying documents and the accounting method before changing the date. The bank posting date alone does not always determine the correct year, particularly when accrual accounting or special tax rules apply.
A view of upcoming cash needs

Accounts receivable tracks money customers owe your business, while accounts payable tracks money your business owes vendors. Both identify amounts that may not yet appear as bank activity. Keeping them accurate supports collections, payment planning and a clearer view of cash commitments.

After a month is reviewed, the completed reports and reconciliation records should be saved, important findings explained and unresolved items clearly identified. The business can then use those records to make decisions and begin the next month with a reliable opening position.

An owner contribution generally represents money or property the owner puts into the business, rather than customer sales revenue. It is typically recorded in the appropriate equity account, but a genuine owner loan is different. The entity structure and supporting facts determine the correct accounts and tax treatment.

An unexpected large expense should be traced to the original transaction before you judge the month’s performance. It may be a legitimate cost, a duplicate, a timing issue or a payment that belongs on the balance sheet. The report total shows where to investigate, not the explanation by itself.

Apply a partial customer payment to the specific invoice it relates to and leave the unpaid remainder open. Preserve the original invoice amount and the history of each payment. A partial payment should not create a second sale if the invoice’s revenue has already been recorded.

Ask which records need repair, what work is included, what you must provide, how pricing is determined and how completion will be verified. Also clarify reporting dates, communication responsibilities and whether coordination with your tax preparer is included. Those answers let you compare the proposed work with your business’s actual needs.

Before approving monthly reports, check the period, accounting basis and completeness of the underlying records. Then review material changes and unusual balances. Approval should mean you understand the reports and know which items, if any, remain unresolved, rather than simply accepting a set of totals.

Before changing an opening balance, identify where it came from and why it appears wrong. An opening balance connects earlier activity with the period you are reviewing. Changing it without evidence can hide an old error and make current reports look correct while leaving the history inconsistent.

Before closing the books for the year, check that activity is complete, balances have support and unresolved items are documented. Review the reporting cutoff and accounting basis, then coordinate significant adjustments with the responsible accountant or tax preparer. A calendar ending does not by itself make the records complete.
Before we work on your books.

Before you give the books to your tax preparer, the records should be organized, reconciled and supported by documents. Income and expenses should be clearly categorized, balance sheet accounts should have explanations and unresolved questions should be identified. Tax preparation still requires professional judgment beyond bookkeeping completion.

Begin with the last period that reconciled correctly and work forward until the difference first appears. Comparing statement activity with the account register narrows the search. The difference may come from one entry, several smaller entries or a starting balance, so avoid assuming a single transaction caused it.

Behind every business is someone trying to keep everything moving. Paper Trail brings structure to the financial records, with bookkeeping repair and monthly support that helps the numbers make sense.

Bookkeeping focuses on maintaining organized transaction records and reconciling them with supporting evidence. Accounting is a broader field that can include interpreting financial results, applying reporting standards and making technical accounting decisions. Responsibilities overlap, so the actual service scope matters more than the label alone.

Bookkeeping help becomes useful when incomplete records, unexplained balances or delayed reports start interfering with business decisions. You do not need a certain revenue level to ask for support. Transaction volume, number of accounts and complexity often matter more than sales alone.

Capture business transactions daily or weekly as appropriate, then complete a monthly reconciliation and review. Higher transaction volume, cash activity and urgent collection or payment decisions may require more frequent attention. The routine should keep transactions explainable and information current enough to manage the business.
Catch Up Bookkeeping: Bring Months of Overdue Books Up to Date

Categorize transactions by what they represent and how they affect the business, using a consistent chart of accounts. First determine whether an item is income, expense, asset, liability, equity or a transfer. Only then choose the more specific category that fits the supporting record.

Check completeness by comparing the books with independent records for the entire month, including bank statements, card statements, sales systems and supplier records. A report showing transactions does not prove that all transactions were recorded. Each source needs a defined beginning and ending date.

Closing a bank account does not remove its history from your bookkeeping. Record all final activity, reconcile the closing statement and document where any remaining money went. Keep the account’s records accessible for the applicable retention period, even after the account is no longer used.

Correct old bookkeeping mistakes by tracing the original entry, documenting the proper treatment and reviewing every affected period. Preserve the supporting evidence and correction history rather than hiding a difference in an unexplained current expense. Older corrections can affect reconciliations and information already used for tax filing.

During a bookkeeping review, ask what changed, what remains unresolved and what the reports mean for the business. The most useful questions connect reported totals with the transactions behind them. Begin by confirming the reporting dates, accounting basis and whether all agreed accounts were reconciled.

Expenses can increase when sales increase because serving more customers often requires more labor, materials, shipping, processing fees or other direct costs. Some overhead can also rise as the business grows. The useful question is whether the additional sales leave enough margin after the related costs.

Find the last reliable completed month, then gather bank statements, card statements and other business records for every unfinished period. Work through the backlog in sequence so corrected balances carry forward properly. Maintain a simple current recordkeeping routine while the older work is completed.

If a vendor bill was paid twice, verify that there are two real payments rather than two copies of one entry. A genuine duplicate payment may create a vendor credit or an amount to recover. Recording it as another purchase would generally overstate the expense.

If your old bookkeeping system no longer provides the data, start by checking backups, exports and access options before rebuilding anything. Missing software access does not necessarily mean all records are gone. Banks, vendors, customers and payment systems may still hold parts of the transaction history.

Deposits may include loans, owner funds, transfers and customer payments from earlier periods, so they cannot automatically be treated as current sales.

Keep bookkeeping current during busy seasons by separating frequent record capture from the deeper monthly review. The business can save receipts and identify payments as activity happens, while reconciliation and reports follow a predictable closing routine. Waiting for business to slow down usually makes the record gap larger.

Keep the documents that support the income, expenses, assets and obligations shown in your books. Financial reports summarize transactions, while receipts, invoices, statements and other records explain what actually occurred. An organized tax preparation package needs both the totals and a way to trace their support.

Loan balances should be reviewed monthly to verify that new borrowing, repayments, interest and fees match the lender’s records. This catches differences before they accumulate and keeps the outstanding debt visible. It also helps explain future payments that will continue to use business cash.

Look for a consistent pattern across profit, cash, customer collections and business activity. Rising sales alone do not establish improvement if costs grow faster or customers take longer to pay. Reliable monthly records make it possible to compare performance without confusing growth with timing or bookkeeping errors.

Maintain an unpaid bill list with supplier names, invoice amounts, due dates, credits and payment status. Review bills due next month alongside expected customer receipts and current cash. A profit report alone will not show the timing of every upcoming payment.

Missing bank transactions can be found by comparing a complete bank statement with the bookkeeping register for the same period. A bank feed is useful, but the statement provides a separate record of posted activity. Check for import gaps, disconnected accounts and entries assigned to the wrong account.

Monthly bookkeeping usually brings together transaction review, categorization, reconciliation and financial reporting. The goal is to create a coherent record of the month, with supporting documents and explanations for significant differences. The scope varies with the business, its payment systems and the condition of its existing books.

Monthly reports should be ready on a schedule agreed with the bookkeeper and suited to the business’s document flow. There is no single reporting date that fits every company. The timing depends on statement availability, transaction volume, missing information and the level of review included.

Negative cash in the books needs investigation before the records go to your tax preparer. It may reflect a real overdraft, outstanding payments, missing deposits or an incorrect opening balance. A negative number is a signal to reconcile the account, not a reason to add an unsupported adjustment.

No, a bank feed imports transactions but does not replace reconciliation. Reconciliation compares your recorded activity with a statement for a specific closing date and explains differences. A connected feed can still contain missing, duplicated or incorrectly matched transactions.

No, supplies are commonly consumed in ordinary operations, while equipment may provide value over several periods and be recorded as an asset. The purchase details, tax rules and approved capitalization policy determine the appropriate treatment. Buying both from the same supplier does not make them the same kind of cost.

Their treatment depends on the business structure and supporting facts, so avoid placing all payments to the owner in one operating expense account.

Profit and cash flow describe different parts of your business finances. Learn why unpaid invoices, bills, and timing can leave a profitable business short of cash.
Profit vs. Cash Flow: Where Your Business Money Is Going

Provide bank and card statements, receipts, customer invoices, supplier bills, payment processor reports and explanations for unclear business transactions each month. Include other relevant records, such as loan statements or payroll summaries, when they are part of the agreed bookkeeping scope. The checklist should reflect how your business receives and spends money.

Read a profit and loss statement from revenue through costs to the final profit or loss for a defined period. First confirm the date range and whether it uses cash or accrual accounting. The report describes financial performance, while the bank balance answers a different question about available cash.

Reconcile your business bank account at least monthly against its statement. The IRS specifically recommends monthly checking account reconciliation. Businesses with high transaction volume or tight cash may also review activity more frequently, while still preserving a completed statement reconciliation for each period.

Record customer cash payments when received, with enough detail to connect the receipt to the sale or invoice. Keep a cash receipt record even if the money is not immediately deposited. Depositing the cash later is normally a movement of already recorded money, not a second sale.

Record genuine business bank fees in a consistent expense category and match them to the bank statement. Fees may include account maintenance, wire charges or transaction charges. Keep them separate from loan principal, owner withdrawals and unrelated transfers so the report explains what the bank actually charged.
Revenue is up, cash is down

Revenue measures income from business activity under the accounting basis used, while cash flow measures money moving into and out of the business. Borrowing, unpaid invoices, equipment purchases and owner transactions can change cash differently from revenue. The two figures therefore do not necessarily rise or fall together.

Review recurring charges by vendor, frequency and business purpose, then compare each charge with the services your business still uses. Bookkeeping can identify repeated payments and price changes. Deciding whether a subscription is unnecessary also requires someone who knows the team’s actual use and contract terms.

Reviewing the same core reports each month makes changes easier to recognize. Consistent reports give you a repeatable view of profit, financial position and cash movement. The value comes from comparing like information and investigating meaningful differences, rather than generating a different dashboard every time.

Rules can speed up transaction categorization, but they need clear conditions and regular review. A merchant name alone may not identify what was purchased. Automatic categorization works best for predictable transactions, while unusual, mixed or ambiguous activity should be checked before posting.
SEC, Beginners’ Guide to Financial Statements

Sales tax collected is not always revenue because the treatment depends in part on whether the tax is imposed on the customer or the seller. Taxes imposed on buyers and collected for a taxing authority are generally excluded from income, while taxes imposed on sellers can have different treatment. Keep tax collections identifiable and reconcile them under the rules applicable to the business.

Save the final profit and loss statement, balance sheet, reconciliation reports, detailed transaction records and relevant supporting schedules at year end. Include receivables, payables, loans, assets and owner activity where applicable. Keep the approved versions and any later adjustments so the reported balances can be explained.

The time required depends on the number of unfinished months, transaction volume, account count and quality of the available records. A meaningful timeline follows a review of those factors. The age of the backlog alone does not show how much work is involved.
The year is current but needs review

The year is ready for bookkeeping close when accounts are reconciled or otherwise supported, material discrepancies are resolved and remaining decisions are documented. Check the balances and supporting records behind the reports, including unpaid invoices, bills, loans and owner activity. A completed profit report alone does not establish that the year is ready.

There is no single monthly time requirement that fits every business. A business with a few predictable transactions needs a different routine from one with inventory, employees, customer invoices and multiple platforms. Plan time for both record collection and reviewing the results, even if someone else maintains the books.

Track customer deposits by customer, project, amount and terms, with a clear record of the work or refund still owed. Apply each deposit to the appropriate invoice or refund when its purpose is fulfilled. Accounting and tax treatment depend on the agreement and reporting method, so cash received is not automatically profit.

Track each payment platform from gross customer activity through refunds, fees and adjustments to the net payout received by the bank. Recording only the bank deposit can hide the cost of processing and make sales difficult to reconcile. Each platform should have a clear, consistent record trail.

Track the costs of operating your business, including direct job costs, rent, software, insurance, professional services, bank fees and other business spending. A useful record shows what was purchased, why it related to the business and how it was paid. Recording a cost does not by itself establish a tax deduction.

Transfers can appear as expenses when imported bank activity is categorized as a purchase instead of movement between accounts. A transfer between accounts belonging to the same business generally moves an asset balance, without creating sales revenue or an operating expense. Both sides need to be matched and reviewed.

Uncategorized transactions need investigation before the books can provide a dependable tax preparation package. They may represent ordinary expenses, sales, transfers, loan activity or owner transactions. Leaving everything in a miscellaneous account can distort the reports and hide information the tax preparer needs.

Use a profit and loss statement for the month to understand revenue and expenses on the reporting basis you use. Then review cash separately. The amount deposited into your bank is not automatically the amount earned, and the remaining bank balance is not the same as monthly profit.

Use an accounts receivable aging report supported by a current invoice and payment record. It shows which customers owe money and how long the balances have been outstanding. Before following up, verify that payments and credits have been applied to the correct invoices.

Yes, a year end review should compare payroll reports with the wages, employer taxes, benefits, payments and payroll liabilities recorded in the books. This is bookkeeping reconciliation, while payroll processing and tax filings remain with the responsible payroll provider or tax professional.

Yes, bookkeeping can be completed remotely when records, account access and communication are organized. The essential work is the same, recording transactions, checking supporting documents, reconciling balances and producing useful reports. The location of the bookkeeper does not replace those controls.

Yes, business loans should be recorded and reconciled before records go to your tax preparer. Borrowing normally creates a liability rather than sales income, and each repayment may include principal, interest and fees that need separate treatment.

Yes, comparing monthly expenses can show where costs are changing, provided both months use consistent categories, reporting periods and accounting methods. A larger total is a starting point for investigation, not an automatic sign that the business is spending badly.

Yes, every business credit card account with a balance or activity should be reconciled against its statement. Reconciling only the bank account confirms payments leaving the bank, but it does not prove that individual card purchases, refunds, fees and the remaining card liability are correct.

Yes, for a business with a December year end, cleanup can continue after December as final statements, supplier bills and other records become available. Completing the work later does not move transactions into a different year. The accounting method and underlying facts determine the appropriate period.

Yes, mixed business and personal activity can usually be reviewed and separated when enough supporting information exists. The goal is to identify the purpose of each transaction and record owner activity correctly, rather than treating every charge on a business account as a business expense.

Yes, monthly bookkeeping can reveal slow collections, rising bills, repeated overdraft fees and cash tied up in inventory or equipment. It explains historical cash movement, while a forward cash forecast adds expected collection and payment dates to identify a possible upcoming shortfall.

Yes, prior year bookkeeping can often be completed from bank and card statements, invoices, receipts and other business records. The approach depends on what already exists, which periods are incomplete and whether a tax return for that year has been filed.

Yes, recording the same transaction twice can distort cash, expenses, revenue or liabilities. The effect depends on which accounts the duplicated entry touches. Before removing an entry, confirm that it represents the same real transaction and check whether either version is linked to a bill, invoice or reconciliation.

Yes, review overdue customer invoices at least monthly, and more frequently when collections affect immediate cash needs. Confirm that each balance is still owed and determine the appropriate follow up. An aging report is a useful starting point only when payments and credits are recorded accurately.

Yes, review unpaid supplier bills before closing the month to confirm what remains owed and whether recorded payments match the bills. The review supports cash planning and can affect accrual reports. A business using cash basis reporting also benefits from an accurate schedule of upcoming obligations.

Yes, several months can be corrected within one bookkeeping repair project. The work should follow a clear period sequence because an error in an early balance can carry into every later month. Correcting the supported source of the problem is more useful than patching the latest total.

Yes, unpaid customer invoices matter at year end because they show money still owed to the business and help explain future cash collections. Whether an unpaid invoice affects that year’s reported income depends on the accounting method and the applicable recognition rules.

Yes, unpaid supplier bills identify obligations that may still need payment after year end and help explain future cash needs. Their effect on that year’s expense report depends on the accounting method, the nature of the cost and the supporting facts.

You can begin catching up before every receipt is located, but missing documentation still needs attention. Statements establish payment activity, while receipts and invoices help explain what was purchased and its business purpose. Some expenses require more detailed substantiation than a bank transaction provides.

You can change bookkeeping software during the year, but the migration needs a defined cutoff date, verified balances and access to the original records. Moving data is only part of the job. The new system must reproduce the business’s financial position without duplicating or omitting activity.

You usually do not need to start over, because incorrect balances can often be repaired within the existing bookkeeping file. Missing transactions, duplicates, misclassified transfers and unsupported opening balances are common causes. Review the existing records before deciding whether a rebuild is necessary.

Your bank balance and bookkeeping balance may differ because of timing, missing entries, duplicates or errors. The comparison only becomes meaningful when it uses the same account and date. Reconciliation explains legitimate outstanding items and corrects recording problems so the adjusted balances agree.
